findings.evidence: Wrenford "seto" = two: misheard: theto → seto (generation 21) · Wrenford "li" = six: coined for "wood" by Bram (generation 1) · Wrenford "pabo" = yes: misheard: bobo → babo → pabo (generation 11)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.66, p = 0.023, n = 12. Most used: two (14% replaced per generation), food (10% replaced per generation), wood (13% replaced per generation); least: four (29%), five (78%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 11, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.72, p = <0.001, n = 25.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
